clusters.text: Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government. Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election. Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension. "Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X. No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government. Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government. A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision. Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said. clusters.text: Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen both expect overtaking to be much harder at Interlagos than in previous seasons, as they prepare to start Sunday's Brazilian Grand Prix from the back of the grid. Both drivers have taken new power unit parts in Brazil, exceeding their allocation for the season. As a result, Hamilton and Verstappen will start from 20th and 21st on the grid, respectively, with only Cadillac's Sergio Perez behind them in 22nd. Interlagos has long been a track where overtaking has been relatively easy. Both Verstappen and Hamilton have won at the track from well down the order before: Hamilton from 10th in 2021 and Verstappen from 17th in 2024. But with DRS gone under the 2026 regulations and the new overtake mode, both believe this may no longer be the case. "It's going to be a bit harder to overtake," Verstappen told Sky Sports F1 after the rain-soaked qualifying session. "The overtake mode doesn't really do a lot around here. Everyone is draining their battery from the last corner to Turn 1. Everyone has their wings open. Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images "So the effect is going to be less than normal. And that will make it a bit harder to overtake once you get to the cars that are similar lap time. The first few cars is not a problem, but then the other ones will be a bit harder." Hamilton added while speaking to the media: "I think [it will be] harder. Because back then we had, obviously, a very long straight. And if you got close, you had the DRS and maybe a car wouldn't have it. "Because now everyone is just opening up their wings, I think overtaking will be very, very, very hard. I'm not sure you're going to see the same sort of races that you've seen in the past. But maybe the wet conditions will change that."

clusters.text: A strong earthquake shook central Japan early Sunday, shattering store windows, causing people to flee buildings and leaving at least 22 people injured, according to local media.Japan's Meteorological Agency put the quake's magnitude at 5.7, while the US Geological Survey reported it at magnitude 5.5. Smaller aftershocks were reported.A wide area near Aichi Prefecture was affected, including the city of Hamamatsu, the ancient capitals of Kyoto and Nara and nearby prefectures of Yamanashi, where Mount Fuji is located, as well as Gifu.Japanese TV footage showed shattered store windows and scattered shards of glass on the streets. A bookstore was left with mounds of books that had flown off the shelves. The injuries included people who fell from stairs while they were trying to flee.The quake, which struck at 1:04 am, was located about 40 kilometres below the earth's surface in Shizuoka Prefecture. Aichi and Shizuoka are neighbouring regions. They are far enough from Tokyo that the quake was not felt there. The most violent shaking was felt in Aichi, according to official seismic assessments.The meteorological agency warned people to brace for possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially the next two to three days.“Please be on the lookout for mudslides, falling rocks and the possible effects from rainfall,” Ayataka Ebita, an agency official, told reporters.He said no apparent change was detected so far to the Nankai Trough plate, where scientists say a megaquake can possibly hit.The Shinkansen bullet trains were running at slower speeds in the affected areas as a precautionary measure. He also felt the team management's approach was coming at the expense of KL Rahul's opportunity to spend more time at the crease.Reacting to India's batting order during the second ODI against New Zealand in Wellington, Ganesh took to X to express his reservations about Axar's suitability for the role, particularly in SENA countries (South Africa, England, New Zealand and Australia)."I say it again: Axar Patel can’t be your no 5 in SENA countries. He could play a cameo here and there but he’s definitely not a long term solution. You are denying KL Rahul the game time #NZvIND," Ganesh wrote.The former cricketer's comments come amid India's continued experimentation with their middle-order combinations. The team has often pushed Rahul down to No. 6 to maintain a left-right batting combination, with Axar getting an opportunity higher up the order.That strategy came under scrutiny during the rain-affected second ODI, where India's batting line-up struggled against New Zealand's disciplined pace attack while chasing a target of 135.After the visitors' bowlers had bundled out New Zealand for 134, India found themselves in early trouble on a surface offering bounce and movement. Jacob Duffy struck twice, dismissing captain Shubman Gill for a first-ball duck and Virat Kohli for seven, while Rohit Sharma managed 23 off 28 deliveries before departing.Axar, promoted to No. 5, could contribute only seven runs before falling while attempting a ramp shot. Shreyas Iyer made 30 off 46 balls but failed to convert his start, leaving India under pressure at 47/4.Rahul, meanwhile, provided the stability India desperately needed. Initially cautious, he negotiated the challenging conditions before shifting gears with a couple of pull shots, including a six. He remained unbeaten on 26 as India reached 113/7 in 26 overs when rain brought the contest to an end.India were four runs ahead of the DLS par score at that stage, securing a four-wicket victory and taking a 2-0 lead in the five-match series.The bowling effort had laid the foundation for the win, with Gurnoor Brar claiming career-best figures of 4/30. clusters.text: Enzo Maresca blamed his side’s lack of desire and the way they were outgunned in duels for a third successive Premier League defeat. After winning their first seven games of the season, Manchester City’s 3-1 loss at Nottingham Forest extended their poor run. Jair Cunha dispossessed Josko Gvardiol to score the opener, then Liam Delap struck twice with muscular surges on the break as Forest won their first home league game since April. “Today I think [the problem] has been general,” said Maresca. “It’s not about one player. In the first half we lost all the duels, all the contacts. Against this team, that is fighting relegation, if you don’t match them … it’s something we need to understand. In this kind of game, if you’re not able to win duels and second balls like in the first half, you struggle. “You need desire and intensity to win second balls and duels. You require intensity or you struggle and we didn’t match their intensity. The second and third goals are copy and paste, lost duels first in the middle of pitch then at the edge of the box.” City’s 100% record came to an end with a 2-1 defeat away by Aston Villa , and they followed that up last week with a 1-0 home reverse against Brighton . “They are all different,” said Maresca. “But if you look at chances, possession, chances inside box, in all of them we were much, much better but we lost all of them. We’re going to use this international break to clarify what we can do better. We know we need to improve things and avoid this kind of game.” After his frustrated reaction to last week’s defeat at Brentford , Oliver Glasner was understandably delighted that his reset, ending what he had referred to as compromises, had paid off. “The way we play football I think we’ve had many better games,” he said. “But how we defended, how passionately we defended, how tactically smart we defended, it was one of our better games. “You should control everything and if you want to control it, you have to run because you have to be so quickly aware – they’re so good, such great players, such a good structure and they move the ball so quickly. Of course, you can just defend but you also need to go forward and this is what we did today in the right moments.”
